lessons.title: Security governance and roles
objectives: Tell apart security governance and security management.
Place the roles: board of directors, senior management, security committee, CISO, SOC, auditor.
Tell apart accountability (responsabilité finale) and responsibility (responsabilité d'exécution).
Explain due diligence and due care.

references.title: ISO/IEC 27014:2020, Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection — Governance of information security
COBIT (ISACA), IT governance and management framework

blocks.text: Governing or managing?

Governance sets the direction: it decides on security objectives, risk appetite and resources, then checks that the organization sticks to them. Management executes: it plans, implements and runs day to day the measures that achieve those objectives. In other words, governance answers "are we doing the right things?" and management "are we doing them right?".

rows: Approve the security policy and the SOC budget
Deploy the SIEM and organize on-call duty

blocks.text: ISO/IEC 27014 describes information security governance around processes such as evaluate, direct, monitor and communicate. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 added a "Govern" function to its historical functions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover).

blocks.title: NIST CSF 2.0: "Govern" at the center
blocks.alt: Cycle of the five historical functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, around the Govern function added in version 2.0.

blocks.text: Who does what?

rows: Ultimate accountability for security; sets the risk appetite; approves policy and budget
Arbitrates priorities between business units, follows the action plan and major risks
Runs the security program, advises management, reports on risks
Owners of the risks and data of their activity
Implement and operate the technical measures
Monitors, detects, qualifies and responds to incidents
Independently checks that controls exist and work

blocks.title: Accountability (responsabilité finale)
blocks.text: Obligation to answer for a result. It cannot be delegated: management remains accountable for security even if it entrusts tasks to the CISO or to a service provider.

blocks.title: Responsibility (responsabilité d'exécution)
blocks.text: Duty to carry out a task. It can be delegated: the administrator is in charge of applying patches, the SOC of handling alerts.

blocks.title: Key point
blocks.text: You can delegate execution (responsibility), never ultimate accountability. If a provider applies patches badly, management remains accountable for the result.

Ideally, the CISO reports to a level that guarantees the necessary independence (executive management, risk management). If the CISO reports to the CIO whom they sometimes have to contradict, a conflict of interest can arise.
Due diligence and due care

blocks.title: Due diligence (diligence raisonnable)
blocks.text: Effort to know and understand the risks: gathering information, assessing, auditing, checking a supplier before signing.

blocks.title: Due care (prudence raisonnable)
blocks.text: Acting as a prudent and competent person would: putting in place and maintaining reasonable measures against known risks.

blocks.title: Due diligence or due care?
blocks.text: A memory aid often used in exam preparation: due diligence is about "knowing", due care is about "doing". An organization that has identified a critical flaw (diligence) but does not fix it (lack of care) can be found negligent.

In the exam, look for who "decides" and who "does". Management decides and answers before the law, the CISO advises and steers, the teams execute, audit checks. Putting each actor in the right box is often enough to find the answer.

blocks.title: SOC case: who decides to shut down?
blocks.text: At 2 a.m., the SOC detects encryption in progress on a factory's production server. Shutting the server down stops production. The procedure, approved by management (governance), authorizes the on-call manager to isolate a server in the event of confirmed ransomware. The SOC applies the procedure (management) and informs the CISO, who alerts the plant manager, the risk owner.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I translate risks into business stakes so that management decides knowingly.
SOC manager: I need approved procedures to act fast without waiting for a sign-off in the middle of the night.
Auditor: I check that roles are written down and assigned, and that management really follows the risks.
Risk manager: I make sure that the risk appetite set by management is translated into concrete thresholds.

blocks.title: Good practices
items: Have the security policy approved by executive management, not only by the IT department.
Attach the CISO to a level that guarantees independence from the teams they oversee.
Write down in advance who may decide to isolate a critical system during an incident.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Ultimate accountability for security belongs to executive management, not to the CISO.
Accountability cannot be delegated; responsibility can.
Governance = direct and oversee; management = plan and execute.
Due diligence = gather information, assess; due care = act and maintain.
Governance directs and oversees, management executes.
Management bears ultimate accountability; the CISO steers and advises.
Due diligence (knowing) and due care (doing) underpin the notion of negligence.

lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a ship's wheel next to a compass: governance sets the course.

lessons.title: Information classification and data roles
objectives: Explain the purpose of information classification.
Compare government and commercial classification schemes.
Tell apart the data owner, the data custodian and the user.
Apply least privilege and need to know.

references.title: NIST SP 800-60, Guide for Mapping Types of Information and Information Systems to Security Categories

blocks.text: Why classify?

Not all information deserves the same protection. Classification sorts information into a few levels according to the impact of its disclosure, alteration or loss. Each level comes with rules: who may access it, how to store it, transmit it, label it and destroy it. That way, what matters is strongly protected without weighing down the rest.

blocks.title: Setting up a classification
items: Define the levels and their criteria (management approves them).
Appoint the information owners.
The owner classifies their information.
Attach handling rules to each level (labeling, encryption, sharing, destruction).
Train users and check that the rules are applied.
Review periodically: information can be downgraded or reclassified.

rows: Typical levels (from most to least sensitive)
Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, then Sensitive But Unclassified (replaced since 2010 by CUI, Controlled Unclassified Information) and Unclassified
Confidential (or Restricted), Private, Sensitive / Internal, Public

blocks.text: The names of commercial levels vary from one organization to another: what matters is that each level is defined and associated with rules. In the exam, remember above all the logic and the order of the levels.
Data roles

blocks.title: Data owner (propriétaire des données)
blocks.text: Business manager, usually a senior executive, accountable for protecting a set of information. The owner sets its classification, decides who may access it and approves the measures.

blocks.title: Data custodian (dépositaire)
blocks.text: Often the IT team: applies the owner's decisions day to day (backups, access rights, encryption, restoration).

blocks.title: User (utilisateur)
blocks.text: Person who uses the data as part of their job, following the handling rules.

blocks.title: Who does what with data?
blocks.alt: Three-step diagram: the owner classifies the data and sets the rules, the custodian applies the technical protections, the user follows the rules day to day.

blocks.text: The owner Decides, the custodian Applies, the user Respects: "D.A.R.". The owner is almost always a business manager, not IT.

Two principles complete these roles. Least privilege: everyone receives only the rights needed for their job. Need to know: even with a sufficient clearance level, you only access information if your job requires it.

blocks.title: Two common mistakes
items: Over-classifying: everything becomes "confidential", the rules become impossible to follow and are bypassed.
Under-classifying: sensitive data circulates without encryption or sharing controls.

blocks.title: SOC case: bulk export
blocks.text: The SIEM raises an alert: a salesperson exported 40,000 customer records from the CRM on a Friday evening. The records are classified "Confidential". The analyst checks the rights: the salesperson does have access to the CRM, but a full export is not needed for their job. The SOC escalates to the data owner (sales director), who decides to restrict exports; the custodian (CRM team) applies the change.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: without classification, I cannot size the measures or prioritize the alerts.
SOC manager: the classification level of the affected data sets the severity of the incident.
Auditor: I check that every data set has an owner and an up-to-date classification.
Risk manager: classification directly gives me the impact to use in the risk analysis.

blocks.text: On the SOC side, classification is used every day: an exfiltration alert on a "Public" folder and the same alert on a "Confidential" folder do not have the same priority.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: It is the owner who classifies, not the custodian nor the CISO.
The custodian applies; the custodian does not decide on access.
Least privilege is about rights; need to know is about access to a specific piece of information.
A high clearance does not give access to everything: need to know comes on top.
Classify in order to protect each piece of information according to its impact.
Owner: decides and classifies; custodian: applies; user: follows the rules.
Least privilege and need to know limit access.

lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of three folders with colored labels, from green (public) to red (confidential), and a stamp.

lessons.title: Personnel security, awareness and performance monitoring
objectives: List the security measures before, during and after employment.
Explain separation of duties, job rotation and mandatory vacation.
Tell apart awareness, training and education.

references.title: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1, Building a Cybersecurity and Privacy Learning Program
NIST SP 800-55, Measurement Guide for Information Security

blocks.text: The employee life cycle

blocks.title: The employee life cycle
blocks.alt: Five-step diagram: before hiring, onboarding, during employment, change of role, departure.

rows: Background checks proportionate to the role and compliant with local law, job description that includes security
Non-disclosure agreement (NDA), acceptable use charter, accounts created on a need basis, awareness
Periodic review of rights, continuous training, known disciplinary process
Removal of rights no longer needed (avoid privilege creep)
Immediate deactivation of accounts, return of equipment, reminder of confidentiality obligations

blocks.text: Limiting fraud and abuse

blocks.title: Separation of duties (séparation des tâches)
blocks.text: A sensitive task is split between several people, so that no one can carry it out alone. Fraud then requires collusion.

blocks.title: Job rotation (rotation des postes)
blocks.text: People periodically change roles. This reduces dependence on a single person and allows a successor to detect irregularities.

blocks.title: Mandatory vacation (congés obligatoires)
blocks.text: Requiring an absence of several consecutive days: during that time, a replacement does the work and an ongoing fraud is likely to surface. It is first and foremost a detective control.
Mandatory vacation and job rotation work the same way: someone else takes over the role and sees what was hidden. They are detection controls as much as deterrents.
These measures are combined with least privilege and dual approval (the four-eyes principle). Example: whoever creates a supplier in the ERP cannot approve its payment.
Awareness, training, education

rows: Give a skill for a role

blocks.text: Steering with indicators

blocks.title: KPI, Key Performance Indicator (indicateur de performance)
blocks.text: Measures the performance of a process or a control. Example: mean time to handle a critical alert (MTTR).

blocks.title: KRI, Key Risk Indicator (indicateur de risque)
blocks.text: Signals that a risk is increasing, before it materializes. Example: number of exposed servers missing a critical patch for more than 30 days.
KPI = Performance: "are we doing the job well?" (mean time to handle an alert). KRI = Risk: "is the danger growing?" (exposed servers missing a critical patch).
A good indicator is measurable, useful for a decision and presented to the right audience: management wants trends and risks, the SOC team wants times and volumes.

blocks.title: The orphaned account
blocks.text: An account left active after a departure is an open door: nobody monitors its use, and a malicious login looks like normal activity.

blocks.title: SOC case: the orphaned account
blocks.text: The SOC spots a VPN connection with the account of an employee who left three weeks ago. The account was never disabled: the departure process was not linked to the directory. Measures: immediate deactivation and investigation (SOC), correction of the HR-IT process (management), addition of a KRI "active accounts of people who have left" reviewed every month by the security committee (governance).

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: people are both the first weakness and the first line of detection.
SOC manager: an aware employee who reports a suspicious email is worth a detection rule.
Auditor: I compare the HR list of leavers with the list of active accounts.
Risk manager: KRIs let me alert management before the incident.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Mandatory vacation: main goal = detect fraud, not well-being.
Separation of duties: prevents fraud by a single person; it is defeated by collusion.
Awareness ≠ training: awareness targets everyone and behavior.
A KPI measures performance; a KRI measures how a risk evolves.
Personnel security before, during and after employment, with rights removed on departure.
Separation of duties, job rotation and mandatory vacation fight fraud.
Awareness (everyone), training (roles), education (experts).
KPI for performance, KRI for risk.

lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of an employee badge with a stylized photo, linked to a key and an exit door.

questions.prompt: The board of directors sets risk appetite and approves the security budget. This activity belongs to:
questions.explanation: Setting direction, risk appetite and resources, then overseeing, is the role of governance.

whyNot.0: Management implements the direction; it does not set it.
whyNot.2: The SOC operates detection and response measures; it does not set strategy.
whyNot.3: External audit verifies independently; it does not run the organization.

questions.prompt: Who bears ultimate responsibility for information security in a company?
questions.explanation: Ultimate responsibility (accountability) belongs to senior management, which sets the objectives and allocates resources. The CISO steers and advises.

whyNot.0: The CISO steers the program and reports, but is not ultimately accountable.
whyNot.2: The CIO runs the information system; the CIO is not ultimately accountable for the organization's security.
whyNot.3: The SOC manager is in charge of detection and response, not of overall accountability.

questions.prompt: A company entrusts patching to a managed service provider. What remains with the company?
choices: Only legal responsibility, not operational responsibility
Nothing: responsibility is transferred by the contract
Responsibility for carrying out the patching
questions.explanation: The task (responsibility) is delegated to the provider, but the company remains accountable for the result (accountability).

whyNot.0: This split makes no sense here: the company remains accountable for the overall result, including the operational result toward its customers.
whyNot.1: Accountability cannot be transferred by contract.
whyNot.3: Carrying out the work is precisely what was delegated to the provider.

questions.prompt: Before choosing a hosting provider, a company examines its certifications, audit reports and past incidents. It is exercising:
questions.explanation: Getting informed and assessing before deciding is due diligence.

whyNot.0: Separation of duties splits a sensitive task among several people.
whyNot.1: No risk is being accepted here: the company is getting informed.
whyNot.3: Due care means acting and maintaining reasonable measures, not investigating.

questions.prompt: A company has known for six months that an exposed server has a critical flaw, but does nothing. An incident occurs. Which principle did it mainly fail?
questions.explanation: It knew about the risk (diligence took place) but did not act reasonably: this is a lack of due care, comparable to negligence.

whyNot.0: Need to know limits access to information; it is not at issue.
whyNot.2: The flaw was known: the effort to find out was made.
whyNot.3: Job rotation is an anti-fraud measure unrelated to this case.

questions.prompt: Why is it often recommended that the CISO should not report to the CIO?
choices: To give the CISO access to administrator passwords
Because the law forbids this reporting line in every country
So that the CISO can manage the IT budget
To avoid a conflict of interest when the CISO must report IT department shortcomings
questions.explanation: The CISO oversees and sometimes challenges the IT department's choices (deadlines, patches, exceptions). An independent reporting line protects the CISO's freedom to report risks.

whyNot.0: The reporting line has nothing to do with access to accounts; the CISO does not need these passwords anyway.
whyNot.1: There is no general legal ban: it is an organizational good practice.
whyNot.2: Managing the IT budget is not the goal; the security budget can in any case remain separate.

questions.prompt: Which actor independently verifies that security controls exist and work?
questions.explanation: Internal audit provides senior management with independent assurance on the effectiveness of controls.

whyNot.0: The custodian applies the measures; it cannot audit itself.
whyNot.1: The owner decides how its risks are treated; it is not the independent verification body.
whyNot.2: The SOC operates detective controls; it is not independent of how they work.

questions.prompt: Which of these activities belong to security governance? (2 answers)
choices: Tracking major risks and the progress of the security plan in the executive committee
questions.explanation: Approving the policy and overseeing risks and the action plan are direction and oversight activities: governance.

whyNot.0: Configuring the SIEM is an operational activity (management, operations).
whyNot.3: Applying patches is an operations task.

questions.prompt: Which ISO standard specifically addresses information security governance?
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27014 provides the principles and processes of information security governance.

whyNot.0: ISO/IEC 27035 covers security incident management.
whyNot.1: ISO/IEC 27005 covers information security risk management.
whyNot.2: ISO 22301 covers business continuity.

questions.prompt: At night, the SOC confirms active ransomware on a critical server. What allows the on-call analyst to isolate the server without waiting for senior management?
choices: The verbal agreement of a colleague on the on-call team
The maintenance contract signed with the server's supplier
A response procedure approved in advance by senior management
The analyst's technical expertise and seniority
questions.explanation: Governance delegates in advance, in an approved procedure, the power to act in defined cases. The analyst can thus act quickly and legitimately.

whyNot.0: A verbal agreement between peers is not a delegation of authority.
whyNot.1: The maintenance contract gives no decision-making power over the business.
whyNot.3: Expertise does not give the authority to stop a business activity.

questions.prompt: Who decides the classification level of a payroll file?
choices: The data owner (for example the HR director)
questions.explanation: The data owner, a business manager, sets the classification and decides on access.

whyNot.0: The administrator is the custodian: they apply the owner's decisions.
whyNot.2: The CISO defines the classification framework and advises, but does not classify each piece of information in place of the business.
whyNot.3: Users respect the classification; they do not set it.

questions.prompt: The IT team backs up and restores the customer database according to the rules set by the sales director. What is its role?
questions.explanation: The custodian applies, day to day, the measures decided by the owner: backups, rights, encryption.

whyNot.1: The owner is the sales director, who sets the rules.
whyNot.2: The auditor verifies independently; the auditor does not run the backups.
whyNot.3: The user uses the data for their work; they do not administer it.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of information classification?
choices: Sorting files by creation date and by department
Giving each piece of information protection proportionate to its impact
Reducing the number of servers and file shares
Encrypting all company data in the same way
questions.explanation: Classification makes it possible to strongly protect what is sensitive without needlessly burdening the rest.

whyNot.0: Security classification is not about organizing documents by date.
whyNot.2: Classification does not aim to reduce the number of systems.
whyNot.3: Encrypting everything is neither the goal nor always relevant; the level determines the measures.

questions.prompt: In the US government scheme often cited in the exam, what is the highest level?
questions.explanation: The order is: Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, then Sensitive But Unclassified and Unclassified.

whyNot.0: Confidential is the third classified level.
whyNot.2: SBU is sensitive but unclassified information.
whyNot.3: Secret is below Top Secret.

questions.prompt: An analyst cleared at "Confidential" level asks to read a colleague's internal investigation file, classified "Confidential", out of curiosity. Which principle justifies a refusal?
questions.explanation: The clearance level is enough, but access must also be necessary for the job: that is need to know.

whyNot.0: Job rotation concerns changes of position.
whyNot.1: Separation of duties splits a sensitive operation among several people.
whyNot.2: Due diligence concerns the organization's effort to know its risks.

questions.prompt: A marketing intern is given administrator rights on their workstation "to save time". Which principle is violated?
questions.explanation: Least privilege requires granting only the rights needed for the job. A marketing intern does not need administrator rights.

whyNot.0: Classification concerns information, not the rights on a workstation.
whyNot.1: Job rotation has nothing to do with this case.
whyNot.2: Due care is a general principle of organizational prudence; the specific principle violated here is least privilege.

questions.prompt: What are the responsibilities of the data owner? (2 answers)
choices: Configuring the ACLs on the file server
Setting the classification of the information
Approving requests for access to the information
questions.explanation: The owner decides: classification and access. The custodian carries out: backups and technical configuration.

whyNot.0: Configuring ACLs is a custodian task, according to the owner's decisions.
whyNot.2: Backups are a custodian task.

questions.prompt: Information classified "Confidential" 5 years ago concerns a product that has since been publicly launched. What should be done?
choices: Reclassify it to a higher level as a precaution
Leave it "Confidential": a classification is permanent
Ask the owner to reclassify it to a lower level
questions.explanation: Classification must be reviewed periodically. The owner can declassify information that has become public, which avoids costly and useless protections.

whyNot.0: Overclassifying for no reason increases costs and trivializes the high levels.
whyNot.1: A classification is not permanent: it follows the value of the information.
whyNot.3: Deletion depends on the retention rules, not on declassification.

questions.prompt: For a SOC, what is the classification of the data affected by an incident used for?
choices: Choosing the most suitable investigation tool
Assessing the severity of the incident and the notification obligations
Calculating the retention period of the SIEM logs
Designating the analyst who will handle the ticket first
questions.explanation: The more sensitive the affected data, the greater the impact; classification helps set the severity and know whether to alert senior management, the DPO or an authority.

whyNot.0: The choice of tool depends on the technical nature of the incident, not on classification.
whyNot.2: Log retention is set by a separate policy.
whyNot.3: Assigning an analyst depends mainly on severity and availability; classification feeds severity but designates no one.

questions.prompt: Since the 2021 reform, how many levels does France's national defense secrecy classification have?
choices: Three: Confidentiel défense, Secret, Très Secret
questions.explanation: Since July 1, 2021, the "Confidentiel défense" level has been abolished; Secret and Très Secret remain.

whyNot.0: There are two levels, not just one.
whyNot.1: That was the organization before the 2021 reform.
whyNot.2: France has never had four levels of national defense secrecy under this regime.

questions.prompt: In an ERP, the person who creates a new supplier cannot approve its first payment. Which principle is applied?
questions.explanation: Splitting a sensitive operation between two people prevents fraud by a single person: that is separation of duties.

whyNot.0: Need to know limits access to information.
whyNot.1: Rotation moves people between positions over time.
whyNot.2: Mandatory vacation requires an absence in order to detect fraud.

questions.prompt: From a security point of view, what is the main objective of requiring accountants to take two consecutive weeks of vacation?
choices: Reducing payroll costs during periods of low activity
Respecting the principle of separation of duties
Allowing a replacement to uncover possible fraud
Improving their productivity when they return from vacation
questions.explanation: During the absence, a replacement handles the files: fraud that required daily intervention is likely to surface. It is a detective control.

whyNot.0: It is not a cost-cutting measure.
whyNot.1: Separation of duties is a different principle: it splits an operation among several people.
whyNot.3: Well-being is a side benefit, not the security objective.

questions.prompt: Which situation makes it possible to bypass separation of duties?
questions.explanation: If the two people who must intervene agree with each other, separation of duties no longer protects: that is collusion.

whyNot.1: Awareness does not bypass the measure.
whyNot.2: Rotation rather helps detect long-lasting collusion.
whyNot.3: Encryption has no effect on separation of duties.

questions.prompt: An employee leaves the company on Friday. Which measure is the most urgent?
choices: Disable their accounts and access as soon as they leave
Archive their emails in six months
Have them fill in a satisfaction survey
questions.explanation: An account left active after someone leaves (orphan account) is a classic entry point. Disabling must be immediate.

whyNot.1: Archiving is about retention, not protection against access.
whyNot.2: The policy must be known beforehand, during employment; on departure, the confidentiality obligations are rather recalled.
whyNot.3: An HR survey has no effect on the access risk.

questions.prompt: A simulated phishing campaign sent to all staff is an example of:
questions.explanation: It targets all staff and seeks to change behaviors: it is awareness.

whyNot.0: Training provides a skill tied to a job, for example a SIEM workshop for analysts.
whyNot.1: Education deepens understanding over time, for example a degree program.
whyNot.2: It is not a measure that repairs an incident.

questions.prompt: "Number of Internet-facing servers missing a critical patch for more than 30 days." What type of indicator is this?
questions.explanation: This indicator signals an increase in exposure, before the incident: it is a key risk indicator (KRI).

whyNot.0: An SLA is a contractual service level commitment.
whyNot.2: A KPI measures the performance of a process, for example the average time to patch.
whyNot.3: The RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime, in business continuity.

questions.prompt: Which indicators measure the performance of the SOC (KPIs)? (2 answers)
choices: Number of privileged accounts without MFA
Mean time to detect an incident (MTTD)
Mean time to resolve an incident (MTTR)
Number of critical suppliers not assessed
questions.explanation: MTTD and MTTR measure the effectiveness of the detection and response process: they are SOC KPIs.

whyNot.0: This number signals a risk exposure: it is rather a KRI.
whyNot.3: This number measures a third-party exposure: it is rather a KRI.

questions.prompt: Besides detecting fraud, what benefit does job rotation bring?
choices: It reduces each employee's clearances to zero
It reduces dependence on a single person for a critical task
It removes the need to log employees' actions
It replaces separation of duties in sensitive processes
questions.explanation: Several people know how to do a critical task: the organization depends less on a single expert.

whyNot.0: People keep the clearances needed for their current position.
whyNot.2: Logging is still needed to trace actions.
whyNot.3: Rotation complements separation of duties; it does not replace it.

questions.prompt: An employee has changed department three times in five years and kept all their former rights. What is this phenomenon called and which measure prevents it?
choices: Privilege escalation; antivirus and patches on their workstation
Privilege creep; review of rights at each move
Collusion; mandatory vacation and job rotation
questions.explanation: Rights accumulate with each move. It is prevented by removing unneeded rights at every change of position and by reviewing rights regularly.

whyNot.0: There is no identity theft: it really is the employee who holds the rights.
whyNot.1: Privilege escalation is an attack technique; here the rights were legitimately granted and then never removed.
whyNot.3: Collusion is an agreement between people; that is not the case here.

questions.prompt: When is a new employee asked to sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA)?
choices: Only when they leave the company
When they arrive, before accessing sensitive information
Only if they work in the SOC or the IT department
questions.explanation: The confidentiality commitment is signed on arrival, before the person accesses sensitive information.

whyNot.0: On departure, the obligations are recalled; they must exist beforehand.
whyNot.1: Waiting for an incident is too late.
whyNot.3: Anyone who accesses sensitive information is concerned, not only the SOC.
